Choosing a compute tier: a worked cost example
Starter, Standard, Pro, or Power — the four tiers map to real GPU classes and real hourly rates. Here's the actual math for a chat feature at three traffic levels.
lines.section: Choosing a compute tier: a worked cost example

lines.text: Acmegpu has four compute tiers, and each one maps to a real GPU class rather than an abstract 'small / medium / large' label: Starter runs on an RTX A4000 (16 GB VRAM, $0.40/hr equivalent), Standard on an RTX 4090 (24 GB, $0.60/hr), Pro on an L40S (48 GB, $0.90/hr), and Power on an A100 80GB ($1.20/hr). Those hourly rates are the basis the per-second meter is derived from — you're never actually billed by the hour, only for the GPU-seconds a request consumes.
lines.section: Choosing a compute tier: a worked cost example

lines.text: Say you're shipping a chat feature backed by a 7B-13B instruct model — that's squarely Standard tier territory. Base latency for Standard is 150ms, plus roughly 0.6ms per character of input, plus jitter. A typical 200-character prompt lands around 270ms of GPU time, or 0.27 GPU-seconds. At $0.60/hr, that's $0.60 / 3600 × 0.27 ≈ $0.000045 in compute, plus the flat routing fee of $0.0005/request. Call it $0.00055 per request, roughly 55 cents per thousand requests.
lines.section: Choosing a compute tier: a worked cost example

lines.text: Now scale that up: 10,000 requests a day is about $5.50/day in Standard-tier compute and routing fees combined — before any idle-time savings from scale-to-zero. Bump the same workload to Pro tier (say you moved to a mixture-of-experts model for better answers) and the per-request compute cost roughly 1.5x's, since the rate goes from $0.60/hr to $0.90/hr while latency also tends to grow with model size.
lines.section: Choosing a compute tier: a worked cost example

lines.text: The tier you should pick isn't really a cost question first — it's a 'does this model fit and run fast enough' question. Starter and Standard cover most single-model instruct and embedding workloads. Pro exists for MoE architectures and image models that need more VRAM headroom. Power is for 70B-class models and long-context RAG where 80GB of VRAM is the actual constraint, not a nice-to-have. Once the tier is fixed by what you're running, the per-request math above tells you what to expect on the invoice — and because it's metered per GPU-second rather than per instance-hour, moving a low-traffic endpoint down a tier (or turning on scale-to-zero) shows up in the very next billing cycle, not at the end of a reserved-capacity term.

lines.text: Cold starts, demystified: what happens in that first second
A cold start isn't a black box — here's exactly what's being computed during the 900-1400ms penalty, and when it's worth paying to avoid it.
lines.section: Cold starts, demystified: what happens in that first second

lines.text: When an endpoint has scale-to-zero enabled and hasn't seen traffic recently, its replica count drops to zero — that's the entire point of scale-to-zero, and it's why idle endpoints cost nothing. The trade-off shows up on the next request: before that request can be served, a replica has to come back up, and that has a cost measured in latency rather than dollars.
lines.section: Cold starts, demystified: what happens in that first second

lines.text: On Acmegpu that cold-start penalty is modelled as an additional 900-1400ms added to the request's total latency, on top of the tier's base latency and the per-character processing time. It's applied once, for the request that wakes the endpoint back up — every request after that, until the endpoint goes idle again, runs at normal (warm) latency. The `cold_start` flag on each inference log entry tells you exactly which requests paid that penalty, so you're never guessing whether a slow response was a cold start or something else.
lines.section: Cold starts, demystified: what happens in that first second

lines.text: Whether a cold start matters depends entirely on what's calling the endpoint. A background job or a batch pipeline that fires once every few minutes barely notices an extra second of latency. A user-facing chat feature where someone is staring at a 'thinking...' indicator feels it immediately, especially if it's the first message of a session — which, for a lot of low-traffic apps, is also the most common case, since that's exactly when an endpoint is most likely to have scaled to zero.
lines.section: Cold starts, demystified: what happens in that first second

lines.text: The fix, when a cold start is actually a problem, is straightforward: set minReplicas to 1 (or higher) instead of 0. That keeps at least one replica warm at all times, which means every request skips the cold-start penalty — at the cost of that replica's GPU-seconds accruing continuously instead of only during active requests. It's a real trade, not a free upgrade, so it's worth reaching for only after you've confirmed cold starts are actually showing up in your p95 latency and actually costing you something (a bounced session, a timeout, a bad first impression) rather than reaching for it by default.
lines.section: Cold starts, demystified: what happens in that first second

lines.text: minReplicas, maxReplicas, and what autoscaling actually decides
Two numbers control every endpoint's autoscaling behavior. Here's what each one bounds, what the defaults mean, and how to reason about changing them.
lines.section: minReplicas, maxReplicas, and what autoscaling actually decides

lines.text: Every endpoint on Acmegpu is configured with two numbers that define its autoscaling envelope: minReplicas and maxReplicas. minReplicas is the floor — the fewest replicas that will ever be running, including at zero traffic. maxReplicas is the ceiling — the most replicas that will ever spin up, no matter how much traffic arrives. Everything the autoscaler does happens inside that range.
lines.section: minReplicas, maxReplicas, and what autoscaling actually decides

lines.text: The default when you deploy an endpoint through the API is minReplicas: 0 and maxReplicas: 3, with scaleToZero: true. That combination is tuned for the common case — a new endpoint with unproven traffic that shouldn't cost anything while it's idle, but that can absorb a modest traffic spike (up to 3 replicas' worth of concurrent capacity) without falling over. maxReplicas is capped at 10 platform-wide, and minReplicas can't go negative — the API validates both bounds before an endpoint is created.
lines.section: minReplicas, maxReplicas, and what autoscaling actually decides

lines.text: Raising maxReplicas doesn't cost you anything by itself — replicas only exist, and only accrue GPU-seconds, when there's traffic to justify them. It's purely a safety ceiling for burst capacity. Raising minReplicas above zero is the number that actually changes your baseline cost, because it forces that many replicas to exist continuously, whether or not a request is in flight. That's the direct trade for eliminating cold starts on an endpoint: a permanent floor of GPU-seconds accruing in exchange for consistently warm latency.
lines.section: minReplicas, maxReplicas, and what autoscaling actually decides

lines.text: In practice, most endpoints are well served by the defaults until traffic or latency requirements say otherwise. Watch your endpoint's request volume and p50/p95 latency on its detail page: if maxReplicas is being hit regularly (visible as elevated latency under load, since requests queue for a free replica), raise it. If cold starts are showing up in your p95 more than you can tolerate, raise minReplicas instead of maxReplicas — they solve different problems, and reaching for the wrong one either leaves you paying for idle capacity you didn't need or leaves the cold-start problem exactly where it was.
lines.section: minReplicas, maxReplicas, and what autoscaling actually decides

lines.text: Most 'serverless' GPU offerings still bill an idle instance-hour. Here's why Acmegpu meters per request instead.
A lot of products call themselves 'serverless GPU inference' but still bill you for a warm instance sitting idle. That's not serverless, it's just autoscaling with a marketing label.

Acmegpu's cost model is per active GPU-second: we compute the actual time a request spent on a replica, and that's what gets metered. When an endpoint has scale-to-zero on and no traffic for a while, replicas drop to zero and the meter simply stops. No idle instance-hour, no minimum commitment.

The trade-off is a cold start on the next request after idle — typically under 1.5 seconds on our simulated path. For most app integrations (chat features, background jobs, RAG pipelines) that's a fine trade for not paying for silence.
Every response is labelled — here's exactly what's real (metering, autoscaling state, wallet debits) and what's a demo (the model output).

When you deploy an endpoint on Acmegpu without a live GPU provider configured, every inference call still goes through the full acquire → run → meter → release lifecycle — it just runs a simulated completion instead of a real model forward-pass.

That means: latency is computed from a realistic model (base latency for your tier + a per-character factor + cold-start penalty when idle), GPU-seconds and cost are metered against that latency, and your wallet is genuinely debited. What's simulated is only the text content of the response, and it's labelled '[SIMULATED — demo response]' every time.
This lets you build and test the full integration — auth, metering, error handling, cost tracking — before wiring in a live serving backend, without us pretending a mock is something it isn't.
What the two numbers on your endpoint's metrics panel actually tell you, and when to worry.

A wide gap between p50 and p95 usually means cold starts are showing up in your traffic pattern — check the cold_start flag on individual requests. If scale-to-zero is costing you more tail latency than you want, raising minReplicas above zero keeps at least one replica warm at all times (at the cost of it no longer being free while idle).
Both numbers recompute after every request, so they reflect your endpoint's real, current traffic shape rather than a static benchmark.

lines.text: How to stop or cancel your Acmegpu instances and account.

Acmegpu has no subscriptions or recurring charges. You pay only when you use an endpoint. There is nothing to cancel in the traditional sense — simply stop using the service and billing will stop automatically.

You can stop any running endpoint at any time from your dashboard or via the API. Billing stops immediately when the endpoint enters the paused state. You are only billed for the active GPU-seconds your endpoint actually served — a scale-to-zero endpoint accrues $0 while idle.
Paused endpoints retain their configuration (model, autoscaling settings, API key) for 24 hours. After 24 hours, stopped endpoints and their data may be permanently deleted without further notice.

You can permanently delete an endpoint from the dashboard at any time. Deletion is irreversible — the endpoint's configuration, API key, and request logs are destroyed immediately. Billing stops at the moment of deletion.
To close your Acmegpu account, contact us at support@acmegpu.dev with the subject line "Close Account" from your registered email address.

lines.text: How Acmegpu uses cookies and similar technologies.
Cookies are small text files stored on your device when you visit a website. They allow the site to remember information about your visit, such as your login session or preferences.
We also use similar storage technologies such as localStorage for client-side session management.
These cookies are necessary for the Acmegpu platform to function. They cannot be disabled.
Session cookie: keeps you logged in while you use the dashboard. Expires when you close your browser or after a fixed timeout.
CSRF token: protects form submissions against cross-site request forgery attacks.
Cookie consent: stores your cookie preferences (in localStorage) so we do not ask again on every visit.
These cookies help us understand how visitors use Acmegpu so we can improve the service. They are optional and can be disabled via the cookie banner.
Usage analytics: tracks aggregate page views and feature usage. No personally identifiable data is sent to third parties.

Off by default. If enabled, these would help us measure the effectiveness of a campaign that brought you to the site. They are optional and can be enabled or disabled via the cookie banner at any time.
You can update your cookie preferences at any time by clicking the "Manage Cookies" link in the footer of any page.
You can also control cookies through your browser settings. Note that disabling essential cookies may prevent you from logging in or using certain features.
Acmegpu does not serve third-party advertising cookies. Our payment processing partner may set cookies necessary for secure payment flows; these are governed by their own privacy policy.
We may update this Cookie Policy from time to time. We will notify you of significant changes via email or a notice on the platform.

lines.text: Find answers to common questions about Acmegpu, pricing, endpoints, and the API.

Acmegpu lets you deploy a curated model behind a serverless, autoscaling inference endpoint. You get a URL and an API key, and pay only for active GPU-seconds. Scale-to-zero means an idle endpoint costs nothing.
How is this different from renting a GPU box?

Renting a GPU instance bills you whether or not you're sending traffic. Acmegpu meters per request: GPU-seconds actually spent serving, plus a small routing fee. There's no server to manage, patch, or keep warm yourself.
lines.section: How is this different from renting a GPU box?

lines.text: What do I need to get started?
A Acmegpu account with at least $0.50 in wallet balance to deploy, and any HTTP client (curl, fetch, your app) to call the endpoint once it's live.

Usage-metered prepaid wallet: top up, then each inference call debits GPU-seconds at your tier's rate plus a small per-1,000-requests routing fee. No subscriptions, no per-instance-hour minimum.

Unused wallet credit can be refunded within 14 days of purchase. Contact support@acmegpu.dev for refund requests.
What happens if my wallet hits $0?
The affected endpoint pauses automatically. Inference calls return HTTP 503 with a top-up prompt. Resume it from the dashboard once you've topped up.

lines.text: How Acmegpu handles payments, credits, and billing.

Acmegpu operates on a prepaid credit model. You must add credits to your account before deploying any endpoint. Credits are deducted per active GPU-second while an endpoint is in the running state, plus a small per-1,000-requests routing fee. There are no monthly fees, subscriptions, or minimum commitments.

We accept CardA and CardB credit and debit cards. All payments are processed by our secure payment processor and are PCI-DSS compliant — we do not store your full card details on our servers. All prices and transactions on Acmegpu are denominated and charged in US Dollars (USD).
There is no minimum credit top-up amount — add any amount you like. Credits do not expire while your account is active.

Usage is billed per active GPU-second. The per-second rate is derived from the hourly $/hr rate of your selected GPU configuration. Billing begins the moment an endpoint transitions to the running state and stops immediately when the endpoint is paused or deleted. Scale-to-zero endpoints accrue $0 while idle.

If your credit balance reaches $0 while an endpoint is running, the endpoint is automatically paused to prevent negative balances — inference calls return HTTP 503 until you top up and resume it. Endpoint configuration is preserved for 24 hours after an automatic pause, after which data may be permanently deleted.
We recommend enabling low-balance email alerts in your account settings to avoid unexpected interruptions.

Endpoint pricing is displayed in USD on the pricing page and in the dashboard before deployment. Prices may change with notice. Changes do not affect credits already purchased — your existing credit balance retains its face value.
The USD price you see at checkout is the full amount charged to your card, with nothing added on top. Acmegpu does not itemize or add any further charges as part of a purchase.
For billing questions, contact us at support@acmegpu.dev.

lines.text: How Acmegpu collects, uses, and protects your personal data.
Account information: name, email address, and hashed password when you create an account.
Billing information: payment method details are collected and processed by our secure payment processor. We store transaction IDs and credit balances but never store full card numbers.
Endpoint & usage data: deployed endpoint configuration (model, compute tier, autoscaling settings), request counts, latency, and GPU-second metering needed to operate and bill the service.

Request metadata: we log prompt length, latency, and cost for metering and abuse protection. Prompt/response payload content is not retained beyond what metering needs, and is never used to train our models.
Technical data: IP address, browser type, and device information collected automatically when you visit our site.
To provide, operate, and maintain the Acmegpu service.
To process payments and manage your credit balance.
To send transactional emails such as verification codes, password resets, low-balance warnings, and billing receipts.
To monitor for abuse, fraud, and security threats.
To improve the service based on aggregate usage patterns.
We share data with the following categories of third parties only as needed to operate the service:

Infrastructure provider: when a live GPU provider is configured for a deploy, endpoint configuration is shared to provision serving capacity. We never name the underlying provider in user-facing copy.
Payment processor: processes all payments. Your payment details are handled directly by our secure payment processor and subject to their privacy policy.
Email delivery provider: delivers transactional emails (verification codes, receipts, low-balance alerts) on our behalf. Your email address is shared with this provider solely to send those messages.

We retain your account data for as long as your account is active. A paused endpoint's configuration and API key are preserved for 24 hours after pausing, then may be deleted. If you delete your account, we remove your personal data within 30 days, except where we are required by law to retain it (e.g., billing records for tax purposes).
Access: you can request a copy of the personal data we hold about you.
Correction: you can update your account information at any time from your dashboard.
Deletion: deployed endpoints, API keys, and request logs are yours to delete anytime from the dashboard; deleting your account removes the rest.
Portability: request an export of your data as JSON at any time by contacting support — account, endpoints, and billing ledger.
EU region: an EU data region is available on request for customers who need in-region processing.

We use industry-standard security measures including encrypted connections (TLS), hashed passwords, and secure infrastructure. However, no method of transmission or storage is 100% secure. If you discover a vulnerability, please contact us at security@acmegpu.dev.
For privacy-related questions or requests, contact us at privacy@acmegpu.dev.

lines.text: How Acmegpu protects your account, API keys, and data.

Every endpoint gets a unique, high-entropy key. Rotating a key invalidates the old one immediately — nothing keeps working on a revoked key. Keys are scoped to a single endpoint, so a leaked key can't touch the rest of your account.
All traffic to the dashboard and the public inference API is served over TLS. Passwords are hashed (bcrypt); we never store plaintext credentials.

Endpoint configuration, request metrics, and billing history are scoped to your account. Prompt/response payload content is not retained beyond what metering needs, and is never used to train our models.
Public inference endpoints are rate-limited by default. We monitor for abuse patterns consistent with our acceptable-use policy and can pause an endpoint that's being misused.
Card top-ups run through our secure payment gateway. We never see or store full card numbers, and the wallet balance you see is the source of truth for what you owe.
Found a security issue? Email security@acmegpu.dev with details and we'll respond within 48 hours. Please don't test against endpoints you don't own.

lines.text: Terms and conditions for using the Acmegpu serverless GPU inference platform.

Acmegpu lets you deploy a curated model behind an autoscaling inference endpoint: a URL and an API key, metered per active GPU-second. When no live GPU provider is configured for a deploy, the endpoint runs a SIMULATED inference path — every response is clearly labelled as a demo, but metering and wallet debits are real.
Acmegpu is offered to individual developers, not companies — accounts are personal to the individual who registers them, and access is not licensed to organizations as a seat-based or team product.
You must be at least 18 years old to create an account.
You must provide accurate and complete information during registration.
You are responsible for maintaining the security of your account credentials and API keys.
You are responsible for all activity that occurs under your account and your API keys.
Acmegpu uses a prepaid wallet. You top up credits and usage is deducted per request: active GPU-seconds at your tier's rate, plus a small per-1,000-requests routing fee.
All payments are processed by our secure payment gateway. By adding credits, you agree to their terms of service.
Scale-to-zero endpoints accrue $0 while idle — there is no per-minute or per-hour idle charge.
Credits are non-refundable once used. Unused credits never expire and may be refunded within 14 days of purchase upon request.
If your wallet balance reaches $0, the affected endpoint is automatically paused. Inference calls return HTTP 503 until you top up and resume it.
A paused endpoint's configuration, API key, and request history are preserved for 24 hours, then may be permanently deleted.

Deploying a model you do not have the rights to serve. By deploying, you attest you have the necessary rights to the model and any data you send it.

Public endpoints are rate-limited and monitored for abuse by default. We reserve the right to suspend or terminate accounts or pause endpoints that violate this policy without prior notice and without refund.

We target high availability for endpoint serving but do not guarantee uninterrupted service. In the event of extended downtime caused by our platform, affected users will receive automatic credit for the duration of the outage.

You may close your account at any time from your dashboard or by contacting support.
We may suspend or terminate your account immediately if you violate these terms, engage in abusive behavior, or fail to maintain a valid payment method when required.
Upon termination, running endpoints are paused, API keys revoked, and data deleted per our Privacy Policy. Unused credit refunds upon termination are at our sole discretion.
